# FDG8004

> CONSIDER using jagged arrays instead of multidimensional arrays.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 8.1 Arrays.

## How it is checked

- Check: sdk (full coverage)
- Diagnostics: CA1814
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library suggestion, application suggestion, test suggestion
- Status: verified

CA1814 reports multidimensional arrays in parameters, return types, fields and local variables (probe with SDK 10.0.402). The Abrams annotation limits them to problem areas that are multidimensional by nature, such as matrix multiplication; such reports are acceptable and can be suppressed. CA1814 has no code fix, and changing a parameter, return or field type of a public member changes its signature, so the fix is breaking.

## From the book

A jagged array is an array with elements that are also arrays. The arrays that make up the elements can be of different sizes, leading to less wasted space for some sets of data (e.g., sparse matrix) compared to multidimensional arrays. Furthermore, the CLR optimizes index operations on jagged arrays, so they might exhibit better runtime performance in some scenarios.

```csharp
// jagged arrays
int[][] jaggedArray = {
   new int[] {1,2,3,4},
   new int[] {5,6,7},
   new int[] {8},
   new int[] {9}
};

// multidimensional arrays
int [,] multiDimArray = {
  {1,2,3,4},
  {5,6,7,0},
  {8,0,0,0},
  {9,0,0,0}
};
```

> **Brad Abrams:** In general, I have found that usage of non-SZ (one dimension, zero lower bound) arrays in mainstream public APIs is very rare. Their usage should be constrained to problem areas that inherently lend themselves to multidimensional cases (such as matrix multiplication). All other usages should prefer defining a custom data structure or passing multiple arrays.
